title_original: Spain and Austria lead the way on gender parity in Euro cinema thanks to targeted funding
excerpt_original: France’s Lab Femmes de Cinéma has surveyed a decade of gender equality policies in European cinema

blocks.alt: Carla Simon, Marie Kreutzer,Sandra Wollner, Alauda Ruiz de Azua_Credit David Ruano, Ovidiu Hrubaru-Shutterstock, IMAGO-Starface,IMAGO-ZUMA Press Wire

blocks.text: Source: From l-r:David Ruano, Ovidiu Hrubaru-Shutterstock, IMAGO-Starface,IMAGO-ZUMA Press Wire
Carla Simon, Marie Kreutzer, Sandra Wollner, Alauda Ruiz de Azua

Quotas, financial incentives, and targeted public funding in Spain and Austria are having a positive impact on the number of women directing features and accelerating progress towards gender parity, according to the 10 th annual report from France’s Lab Femmes de Cinéma that examined a decade of gender equality policies in European cinema.
Spain was the only country surveyed with firm gender quotas for film funding, reserving 35% to 40% of feature production support for projects directed by women.

According to Spain’s film agency ICAA, the share of features directed exclusively by women rose from 16.5% in 2021 to 26.1% in 2024, while those involving women in directing or screenwriting increased from 35.5% to 46.5%.

Women’s representation across film professions in Spain also climbed from 26% in 2015 to 38% in 2024, according to industry association CIMA. Spain has extended its measures to screenwriting and development, although films directed by women still have budgets averaging 24% less than those by men.
Success stories include Carla Simón’s Alcarras, which was awarded the Golden Bear at Berlin in 2022, and Alauda Ruiz de Azúa’s Sundays , which won the best film prize at San Sebastian in 2025.

Austria became the first European country to surpass gender parity among film directors in 2025, with women directing 52% of films, according to the European Audiovisual Observatory. Marie Kreutzer’s Gentle Monster screened in competition at Cannes 2026 and is a prominent title in this year’s awards conversation, as is Sandra Wollner’s Everytime, which was a standout film in Un Certain Regard at Cannes in May.

The Austrian Film Institute’s Gender Incentive, introduced in 2019, offers a €30,000 bonus to productions employing women in key creative and technical roles through a points-based scheme, with a further 10% uplift linked to commercial or artistic success.

Austria also introduced Gender Budgeting in 2021, aiming to allocate half of its public film funding to projects involving women directors, writers and producers, from script development through to production.
Slow progress
However, Spain and Austria are the outliers, the report said. The authors warned women will not direct half of Europe’s films until 2062 at the current rate of progress.

While two-thirds of the national film agencies surveyed identified financial incentives as essential to achieving parity, only 12 of the 33 countries have implemented them. Seven of those 12 consider financial measures their most effective intervention.

The 10 th annual report from France’s Lab Femmes de Cinéma examined a decade of gender equality policies, drawing on responses from national film agencies in 33 European countries, with an in-depth focus on France, Austria, the UK, Norway and Spain, alongside interviews with seven European researchers and data from the European Audiovisual Observatory.
In the UK, women directed 21% of locally produced films in 2025, below the European average of 26% and behind France (30%), Spain (27%), and Norway (34%).
The UK averaged 23% between 2020 and 2025 and is one of just three countries, alongside France and Norway, to make certain film funding conditional on meeting equality-related requirements.

Despite progress in Spain and Austria, financial measures remain relatively uncommon across Europe. Nine countries offer bonus schemes based around gender, while Spain is the only country with firm quotas and France is the only one introducing financial penalties.

France introduced its parity bonus in 2019 to reward productions with gender-balanced crews. However, following a decline in female-directed films despite the incentive, the CNC introduced a parity penalty in 2026, set to take effect in January 2027, the CNC confirmed to Screen .
Across Europe, women directed or co-directed 25.8% of films in 2025, up from 19.2% in 2015 but down from a peak of 26.5% in 2023, marking two consecutive years of decline.
The study also identifies a career bottleneck: women directed an average of 29% of debut features between 2015 and 2025, compared with just 23% of subsequent films.

Thirteen of the 33 countries surveyed have yet to introduce concrete gender equality measures. Even where policies are in place, progress remains uneven: ten countries said they had increased women’s representation without significantly changing who holds power in the industry, while 12 reported that advances were limited to certain professions or levels of seniority.
“The solutions exist. Spain and Austria prove it. All that is missing is political will,” said Fabienne Silvestre, co-founder and director of Lab Femmes de Cinéma.
“2062 is 36 years away. A young woman leaving film school today will have almost finished her career by the time parity is finally achieved. That is unacceptable,” she added.

The Lab is calling for stronger gender criteria in public funding, greater access for women to production budgets and decision-making positions, and legislative safeguards to protect equality policies.
